Diseases of Immunity

The lecture organizes the laboratory session around hypersensitivity diseases, autoimmune diseases, and an immune-related deposition disorder. Recognition depends on matching clinical clues with characteristic gross or microscopic lesions and, when applicable, special procedures such as electron microscopy, immunofluorescence, PAS, Congo red, and polarizing microscopy. pp. 2–3, 55

Must KnowHypersensitivity types are differentiated by immune mechanism.
Type I uses IgE and mast-cell mediators.
Type II uses IgG or IgM against target cells or tissues.
Type III uses deposited antigen-antibody complexes with complement and leukocyte recruitment.
Type IV is T cell-mediated. p. 12
Hypersensitivity disease

Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis

The lecture case is a 10-year-old boy with malaise, fever, oliguria, and hematuria one month after untreated impetigo. p. 5

Clinical pattern pp. 6–7

  • Occurs most frequently in children 6 to 10 years of age.
  • May present with malaise, fever, hematuria, proteinuria, edema, hypertension, and oliguria.
  • Appears 1 to 4 weeks after streptococcal infection of the pharynx or skin.
  • Lecture oliguria thresholds: infants less than 1 mL/kg/hr. Children less than 0.5 mL/kg/hr. Adults less than 400 mL/day.

Other infection associations p. 7

  • Bacterial: staphylococcal endocarditis, pneumococcal pneumonia, meningococcemia.
  • Viral: hepatitis B, hepatitis C, mumps, HIV infection, varicella, infectious mononucleosis.
  • Parasitic: malaria and toxoplasmosis.

Type III immune mechanism

1. Immune complexes form
Protein antigen triggers antibodies. Antibody reacts with circulating antigen.
2. Complexes deposit
Medium-sized complexes formed in slight antigen excess are described as most pathogenic.
3. Complement activates
C3a and C5a are released. Macrophages and neutrophils are recruited.
4. Tissue injury follows
Inflammatory damage may produce vasculitis, arthritis, and glomerulonephritis.
Clinical CueGlomeruli and joints are highlighted as sites where immune complexes often deposit because blood is filtered at high pressure. p. 11

Microscopic recognition

Normal vs pathologic glomerulus
NormalPathologic
Normal size and diameter.
Lumen is appreciable and proportional.		Hypercellularity.
Neutrophils predominate.
Increased cytoplasmic eosinophilia.
Proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells.

Hypersensitivity disease

Tuberculosis

The lecture case features a 45-year-old diabetic male with afternoon low-grade fever, hemoptysis, anorexia, malaise, easy fatigability, and a cavitary nodular density in the right upper lobe. p. 15

Definition and usual implantation p. 16

  • Communicable chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Usually involves the lungs but may affect any organ or tissue.
  • Inhaled bacilli usually implant in distal air spaces in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe, typically near the pleura.

Tissue injury cell p. 24

  • The primary cell involved in tissue injury is the activated macrophage.
  • Th1 CD4+ T cells release IFN-γ and activate macrophages.
  • Activated macrophages release ROS, RNS, and proteolytic enzymes that kill bacilli but also cause tissue destruction, caseous necrosis, and cavitation.

Pathogenesis

M. tuberculosis enters macrophages
It prevents lysosome-phagosome fusion, allowing persistence and proliferation.
Antigen presentation
Dendritic cells and macrophages present processed antigens to CD4+ T cells. IL-12 is emphasized.
Th1 response
Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ, crucial for macrophage activation.
Granuloma and caseation
The Th1 response orchestrates granuloma formation and caseous necrosis.

Gross and histologic recognition

Must KnowCaseous necrosis is eosinophilic, amorphous, and granular at the center of the lesion.
Grossly it is soft, friable, whitish-gray, cheese-like, and easily crumbles.
Histologically there is no preserved tissue architecture. p. 22
Key DifferentiatorLanghans giant cells are multinucleated cells with a peripheral horseshoe arrangement of nuclei.
Epithelioid cells are activated macrophages with abundant cytoplasm and elongated nuclei. p. 19
HypersensitivityTuberculosis is associated with Type IV delayed T cell-mediated hypersensitivity.
Other lecture examples include rheumatoid arthritis, contact dermatitis, multiple sclerosis, type 1 diabetes mellitus, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. p. 23
Hypersensitivity disease

Asthma

The case centers on a 17-year-old who develops chest tightness, wheezing, and progressive dyspnea during warm-up after a hot bus ride and on a windy field. pp. 25, 27

Pertinent case data p. 27

  • 17-year-old male.
  • Hot and long 45-minute bus ride.
  • Windy field.
  • Symptoms started as the warm-up period was ending.
  • Chest tightness, wheezing, progressive dyspnea.

Additional clinical data to ask pp. 28–29

  • Family history.
  • Medications.
  • Previous episodes.
  • Allergies.
  • Recent illness or underlying medical conditions.
  • Lifestyle.

Normal vs pathologic nasal mucosa

Normal mucosa p. 30

  • Epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells.
  • Lamina propria has few cells and vessels.
  • Basement membrane is thin.

Pathologic mucosa

  • Epithelium shows sloughing.
  • Goblet cells, eosinophils, plasma cells, and edema are present.
  • Basement membrane is thick due to prolonged eosinophil-predominant inflammation.

Type I mechanism

Initial exposure
Respiratory mucosal APCs capture allergen and present it to naive CD4+ T cells.
Th2 differentiation
Th2 cells produce cytokines including IL-4, IL-5, and IL-10.
Subsequent exposure
Re-exposure causes IgE-mediated mast-cell activation.
Early phase
Histamine and leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 produce bronchoconstriction, inflammation, and edema.
Late phase
Inflammation and major basic protein damage cells and worsen bronchoconstriction.
Case Trigger ChainExercise + wind + dust → allergen recognition by IgE on mast cells → mast-cell degranulation → histamine and leukotrienes → airway bronchoconstriction.
Inflammation contributes to airway swelling. p. 32
Autoimmune disease

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus

The lecture case describes fever, facial rash, a mitral-area diastolic murmur, palpable spleen, mild anemia, leukopenia, positive LE cell test, high anti-dsDNA titers, later hypertension, leg swelling, proteinuria, hematuria, elevated BUN, and elevated creatinine. p. 33

Must KnowHallmark: production of antinuclear antibodies.
Anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are emphasized as diagnostic antibodies in the lecture.
Pathology is dominated by immune complex deposition with prominent vasculitis and fibrinoid necrosis. p. 34

Clinical manifestations p. 35

  • Skin lesions such as malar or butterfly rash and discoid rash.
  • Immune complex deposition.
  • Kidney lesions or lupus nephritis.
  • Cardiac lesions.

Antibody studies p. 42

  • ANA: screening test.
  • Anti-dsDNA: high specificity.
  • Anti-Sm: most specific antibody for SLE in the lecture.

Lupus nephritis morphology

Expected pathologic responses p. 37

  • Hypercellularity: increased mesangial, endothelial, or visceral epithelial cells. Leukocytes may infiltrate.
  • Basement membrane thickening: capillary loop walls thicken and capillary lumen caliber decreases.
  • Hyalinosis or sclerosis: pink hyaline is deposited in the mesangial matrix.

Wire-loop lesion pp. 38, 41

  • Rigid thickening of peripheral capillary loops.
  • Due to hyaline or subendothelial immune deposits.
  • PAS is used to highlight basement membranes of glomerular capillaries.
HypersensitivitySLE may show a Type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by immune complex deposition, especially in the kidneys. p. 40
Autoimmune disease

Rheumatoid Arthritis

The case describes bilateral pain and swelling involving wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and ankles, with warm tender joints and subcutaneous nodules near the elbow. Laboratory findings include anemia, hypergammaglobulinemia, and rheumatoid factor. p. 43

Core pathology p. 44

  • Chronic inflammatory disease primarily affecting joints with possible extra-articular involvement.
  • Autoantibodies specific for citrullinated peptides are emphasized.
  • Produces a nonsuppurative proliferative and inflammatory synovitis.

Rheumatoid factor p. 44

  • Lecture defines rheumatoid factor as IgM and IgA autoantibodies that bind Fc regions of IgG.
  • These may be deposited in joints as immune complexes.

Gross and microscopic recognition

Microscopic patterns
Synovium or pannusRheumatoid nodule
Hyperplastic synovial lining with proliferating fibroblast-like synoviocytes.
Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.
Early granulation tissue erodes cartilage and bone.		Central zone: amorphous eosinophilic fibrinoid necrosis.
Middle zone: palisaded macrophages or epithelioid cells.
Outer zone: lymphocytes and plasma cells.
Cell-mediated responseThe lab exercise identifies CD4+ T helper cells as the cells that initiate the autoimmune response and characterizes the hypersensitivity response as cell-mediated. pp. 62–67
Immune-related deposition disorder

Amyloidosis

The case is a 57-year-old male with difficulty eating and talking, weight loss, fatigue, slurred speech, and an enlarged thickened tongue with restricted movement and dental impressions. A biopsy and special stain with polarizing microscopy are requested. p. 47

Gross and microscopic appearance

What is deposited p. 49

  • Extracellular deposits of misfolded fibrillar proteins.
  • These deposits are described as insoluble and non-degradable by macrophages or proteasomes.
  • Normal proteins may misfold when produced in increased amounts or when degradation is impaired.
  • Variant proteins may be prone to misfolding and aggregation.

Cause of tissue damage p. 52

  • Abnormal fibrillar proteins accumulate extracellularly when normal clearance mechanisms fail.
  • The deposits cause tissue damage because the body cannot clear them away.
  • If deposits are limited to one tissue or organ, the case is classified as localized amyloidosis.

Special stain and polarizing microscopy

Macroglossia differentials from the lecturePseudomacroglossia may result from low palate, enlarged tonsils, oral cavity tumors, abnormalities of mandibular or maxillary arches, or hypotonia.
Other categories include tumors and vascular malformations, endocrine abnormalities and congenital syndromes, other deposition diseases, trauma, allergies, and infections. p. 50
Other organsChronic inflammatory disorder-associated amyloidosis may involve kidneys, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, adrenals, and thyroid.
Plasma cell proliferation-associated amyloidosis may involve heart, gastrointestinal tract, respiratory tract, peripheral nerves, skin, tongue, and pancreas. p. 53

Cram Sheet

Gross + histology pictures are intentionally included here so you can switch between text recall and visual recognition without leaving the final review tab.

Fastest anchorsPSGN: Type III + hypercellular glomerulus + EM humps + granular lumpy-bumpy IF.
TB: Type IV + caseous granuloma + Langhans giant cells + activated macrophage injury.
Asthma: Type I + IgE and mast cells + eosinophils + thick basement membrane.
SLE: ANA hallmark + anti-dsDNA + anti-Sm + Type III + wire-loop lesions + PAS.
RA: anti-CCP and RF + pannus + fibrinoid necrosis with palisading histiocytes.
Amyloid: amorphous eosinophilic extracellular material + Congo red + apple-green birefringence.
